decks.title: Vector Algebra — Part 1: Vectors, components and the section formula
goals: Find the magnitude, unit vector, direction cosines and direction ratios of a vector
Recognise zero, unit, equal, negative and collinear vectors
Add, subtract and scale vectors in component form
Write the vector joining two points from their position vectors
Find the point dividing a segment internally or externally in a given ratio

slides.heading: Vector Algebra, Part 1
slides.body_md: Quantities with both a size and a direction.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: vectors as arrows with size and direction, magnitude and direction cosines, types of vectors, components and position vectors, and the section formula.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to vector algebra. A push on a door, the path of a drone and the pull of a kite string all have a size and a direction. Such quantities are vectors. In this part you will measure vectors, describe their directions, add them, and locate points that divide a line segment in a given ratio.

slides.heading: What you will learn

visual.alt: A directed line segment from the initial point P at the lower left to the terminal point Q at the upper right, labelled v, with an arrowhead showing the direction from P to Q.
visual.caption: $\vec{v} = \overrightarrow{PQ}$: the length of the arrow is $|\vec{v}|$; the arrowhead gives the direction.

slides.narration: A vector is drawn as an arrow. Its length is the magnitude and its arrowhead shows the direction. By the end of this part you will be able to find the length and direction of any arrow in space, add arrows, and find special points on a segment.

slides.heading: Magnitude and direction cosines
slides.body_md: For $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$, and the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector $\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$.

visual.alt: Table of formulas: the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components; the direction cosines are the components divided by the magnitude and their squares add to 1; direction ratios are any numbers proportional to the components.
visual.caption: Ratios are proportional to the cosines; cosines are fixed.

slides.narration: The magnitude of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components. Divide the vector by its magnitude and you get the unit vector in the same direction. Its three components are the direction cosines, the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the three axes. Their squares always add up to one.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: magnitudes and unit vectors
slides.body_md: Find the magnitude and direction cosines of three vectors.
bullets: Square, add, take the square root
Divide each component by the magnitude
Check: the squares of the cosines add to $1$

visual.alt: Table of three vectors with their magnitudes and direction cosines: 2 i minus 6 j plus 3 k has magnitude 7, 4 i plus 4 j minus 7 k has magnitude 9, and i minus 2 j plus 2 k has magnitude 3; each direction cosine is a component divided by the magnitude.
visual.caption: Direction cosine = component ÷ magnitude.

slides.narration: Here are three vectors. For the first, the squares of two, minus six and three add to forty nine, so the magnitude is seven, and the direction cosines are two sevenths, minus six sevenths and three sevenths. Notice that the signs of the components carry over to the cosines.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal angles with the axes
slides.body_md: A beam makes equal acute angles with the three axes. What is each direction cosine?
slides.narration: Use the fact that the squares of the three direction cosines add up to one.

slides.heading: Types of vectors
slides.body_md: Some vectors have special names.

rows: one is a scalar multiple of the other

visual.alt: Table of types of vectors: the zero vector has magnitude 0, a unit vector has magnitude 1, equal vectors share magnitude and direction, the negative of a vector reverses its direction, and collinear vectors are scalar multiples of each other.
visual.caption: Collinear vectors may point the same way or opposite ways.

slides.narration: The zero vector has no length and no definite direction. A unit vector has length one. Equal vectors have the same length and the same direction, wherever they are drawn. The negative of a vector has the same length but points the other way. Collinear vectors lie along parallel lines: one is a number times the other.

slides.heading: Adding vectors
slides.body_md: Place the tail of $\vec{b}$ at the head of $\vec{a}$; the arrow from the first tail to the last head is $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$.

visual.alt: Triangle law of addition: an arrow a from O to A, followed by an arrow b from A to B; the arrow from O straight to B closes the triangle and is the sum a plus b.
visual.caption: Triangle law: $\overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB}$.

slides.narration: To add two vectors, place the second arrow so that it starts where the first one ends. The single arrow from the very start to the very end is the sum. This is the triangle law. The same sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram built on the two arrows.

slides.heading: Quick check: a combination of two vectors
slides.body_md: Find two times one vector minus three times another.
slides.narration: Scale each vector first, then subtract component by component.

slides.heading: Components and operations
slides.body_md: In components every operation works one direction at a time.

visual.alt: Table of operations on vectors in components: the sum adds components, the difference subtracts them and a scalar multiple multiplies each component, illustrated with a equals i plus 2 j minus k and b equals 2 i minus j.
visual.caption: Work with each of $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ separately.

slides.narration: Once vectors are written with i, j and k, adding, subtracting and scaling are easy: work with each direction separately. Add the i parts, add the j parts, add the k parts. To multiply by a number, multiply each part by that number.

slides.heading: Position vectors
slides.body_md: The position vector of a point $A$ is $\overrightarrow{OA} = \vec{a}$. Then $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$.

visual.alt: Position vectors from the origin O: an arrow a to the point A and an arrow b to the point B; the arrow from A to B is b minus a, head minus tail.
visual.caption: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$.

slides.narration: The position vector of a point is the arrow from the origin to that point; its components are the coordinates of the point. The arrow from A to B is then the position vector of B minus the position vector of A. Remember the phrase head minus tail.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a vector joining two points
slides.body_md: Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and its length for $P(2, -1, 4)$ and $Q(5, 3, -2)$.
bullets: Subtract the coordinates of $P$ from those of $Q$

visual.alt: Worked example table: from P at 2, minus 1, 4 to Q at 5, 3, minus 2 the vector PQ is 3 i plus 4 j minus 6 k, found as head minus tail, with length root 61.
visual.caption: Always subtract the starting point from the end point.

slides.narration: Subtract the starting point from the end point, coordinate by coordinate. Five minus two is three, three minus minus one is four, and minus two minus four is minus six. The length is the square root of nine plus sixteen plus thirty six, which is the square root of sixty one.

slides.heading: The section formula
slides.body_md: A point $R$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $m : n$. Internally it lies between $P$ and $Q$; externally it lies on $PQ$ produced.

visual.alt: Section formula: a segment from P to Q with the point R on it, splitting it into parts marked m and n; dashed lines from the origin O to P, R and Q show the position vectors p, r and q.
visual.caption: $R$ divides $PQ$ internally in $m : n$ (drawn for $2 : 1$).

slides.narration: Suppose a point R lies on the line through P and Q, and its distances from P and from Q are in the ratio m to n. If R is between P and Q the division is internal. If R lies outside the segment, on the line extended, the division is external.

slides.heading: Section formulae
slides.body_md: Weights go to the far end.

visual.alt: Table of the section formulae: internal division in m to n gives m q plus n p over m plus n, between P and Q; external division gives m q minus n p over m minus n, outside the segment; the midpoint is p plus q over 2.
visual.caption: The weight $m$ goes with the far end $Q$.

slides.narration: For internal division, multiply the far end Q by m and the near end P by n, add, and divide by m plus n. For external division, subtract instead of adding, and divide by m minus n. The midpoint is the special case where m and n are equal.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: internal and external division
slides.body_md: Divide $PQ$ in the ratio $2 : 3$, for $P(1, -2, 3)$ and $Q(6, 8, -2)$, both ways.
bullets: Internal: add the weighted vectors, divide by $5$

visual.alt: Worked example table: P is 1, minus 2, 3 and Q is 6, 8, minus 2; dividing PQ internally in 2 to 3 gives the point 3, 2, 1, and externally in 2 to 3 gives the point minus 9, minus 22, 13.
visual.caption: Same weights, different signs and denominators.

slides.narration: With the ratio two to three, the internal point is two Q plus three P, all over five, which works out to the point three, two, one. The external point is two Q minus three P, divided by minus one, which gives minus nine, minus twenty two, thirteen, far beyond P.

slides.heading: Quick check: a midpoint
slides.body_md: Find the midpoint of a footbridge between two pillars.
slides.narration: Add the two position vectors and halve the result.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: collinear points and the ratio
slides.body_md: Show that $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(3, 5, 4)$ and $C(7, 11, 6)$ are collinear and find how $B$ divides $AC$.
bullets: Find two segment vectors from a common point
Show one is a multiple of the other

visual.alt: Worked example table for A at 1, 2, 3, B at 3, 5, 4 and C at 7, 11, 6: AC is 3 times AB, so the points are collinear and B divides AC internally in the ratio 1 to 2.
visual.caption: Collinear points: one segment vector is a multiple of the other.

slides.narration: The vector from A to C is exactly three times the vector from A to B, and both start at A. So the three points lie on one line. B is one third of the way from A to C, so B divides the segment from A to C internally in the ratio one to two.

slides.heading: Quick check: distance between towers
slides.body_md: Find the straight-line distance between two mobile towers.
slides.narration: Find the vector joining the two points, then its magnitude.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Collinear: one vector is a multiple of the other

rows: internal $\dfrac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n}$; external $\dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the magnitude formula, the unit vector and direction cosines, the vector joining two points as head minus tail, and the internal and external section formulae.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up: the magnitude comes from the squares of the components, and dividing by it gives the unit vector and the direction cosines. Collinear vectors are multiples of each other. The vector joining two points is head minus tail. And the section formula locates points dividing a segment, inside or outside it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show the **magnitude** before dividing by it
In the section formula, the weight $m$ goes with the **far end**
For external division, divide by $m - n$

rows: correct weights and signs, then the point
two segment vectors, the multiple, the common point

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: unit vectors and direction cosines need the magnitude shown; a vector of given length needs the unit vector then scaling; section formula answers need correct weights and signs; collinearity needs two segment vectors, the multiple and the common point.
visual.caption: ISC gives step marks: show each line.

slides.narration: Show the magnitude before you divide by it; the examiner gives a mark for it. In the section formula, attach m to the far end. For external division, remember the minus sign and divide by m minus n. When you prove points collinear, say that the two vectors share a common point.

decks.title: Vector Algebra — Part 2: Scalar and vector products
goals: Find the scalar product in components and use it for angles
Find the vector product and unit vectors perpendicular to two vectors
Find areas of triangles and parallelograms and test collinearity with the vector product

slides.heading: Vector Algebra, Part 2
slides.body_md: Two ways to multiply vectors.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the scalar product, angles and perpendicular vectors, projections, the vector product, and areas and collinearity.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Vectors can be multiplied in two ways. The scalar product gives a number and measures how much two vectors point the same way. The vector product gives a new vector, perpendicular to both. Together they let you find angles, projections and areas.

slides.heading: The scalar product
slides.body_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$.

visual.alt: Table of properties of the scalar product: its definition with the cosine of the angle, the component formula, commutativity, the dot product of a vector with itself equal to its magnitude squared, the products of unit vectors, and the test for perpendicular vectors.
visual.caption: The answer is a number (a scalar).

slides.narration: The scalar or dot product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them. In components it is simply the sum of the products of matching components. The result is a number, not a vector, and the order of the two vectors does not matter.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the angle between two vectors
slides.body_md: Find the angle between $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the angle between i plus 2 j plus 2 k and 2 i minus j plus 2 k: the dot product is 4, both magnitudes are 3, so the cosine of the angle is 4 over 9.
visual.caption: Divide the dot product by the product of the magnitudes.

slides.narration: Multiply matching components and add: one times two, plus two times minus one, plus two times two, gives four. Both vectors have magnitude three. So the cosine of the angle is four divided by nine, and the angle is the inverse cosine of four ninths.

slides.heading: Quick check: a scalar product
slides.body_md: Find the scalar product of two vectors stored by a fitness app.
slides.narration: Multiply matching components, then add the three products.

slides.heading: Perpendicular vectors
slides.body_md: For non-zero vectors, $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b} \iff \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$.

visual.alt: Table of properties of the scalar product: its definition with the cosine of the angle, the component formula, commutativity, the dot product of a vector with itself equal to its magnitude squared, the products of unit vectors, and the test for perpendicular vectors.
visual.caption: The answer is a number (a scalar).

slides.narration: When two non-zero vectors are at right angles, the cosine of the angle is zero, so their dot product is zero. The test also works the other way: a zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular. This is the quickest way to check a right angle in space.

slides.heading: Projections
slides.body_md: The scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $|\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

visual.alt: Projection: vector a from O to A makes an angle theta with vector b along the base line from O to B; a dashed perpendicular from A meets the base at M with a right angle, and the length OM is the projection of a on b.
visual.caption: $OM = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

slides.narration: Drop a perpendicular from the tip of a onto the line of b. The length from the origin to the foot is the scalar projection of a on b. It equals the dot product divided by the magnitude of b. Multiply it by the unit vector along b to get the vector projection.

slides.heading: Quick check: a zero dot product
slides.body_md: Is a dot product of zero enough to say two vectors are zero?
slides.narration: Think of two perpendicular arrows that are not zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: scalar and vector projections
slides.body_md: Project $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ on $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table of projections with an example: the scalar projection of a on b is the dot product divided by the magnitude of b, here minus 2; the vector projection is the dot product over the square of the magnitude times b, here minus two thirds of b.
visual.caption: A negative projection means an obtuse angle.

slides.narration: The dot product is minus six and the magnitude of b is three, so the scalar projection is minus two. The minus sign tells you the angle between the vectors is obtuse. For the vector projection divide by the square of the magnitude, nine, and multiply by b.

slides.heading: The vector product
slides.body_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to both, by the right-hand rule.

visual.alt: Table of properties of the vector product: its magnitude uses the sine of the angle, it is perpendicular to both vectors by the right-hand rule, reversing the order changes the sign, the cyclic products of the unit vectors, and the product of parallel vectors is the zero vector.
visual.caption: The answer is a vector.

math: \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
slides.narration: The vector or cross product of two vectors is a new vector. Its length is the product of the magnitudes and the sine of the angle, and it points at right angles to both vectors, following the right-hand rule. Swapping the order reverses it. In components it is the expansion of a three by three determinant.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a cross product
slides.body_md: Find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ for $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$.
bullets: Write the determinant with $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ on top
Expand along the first row; mind the minus sign for $\hat{j}$

visual.alt: Worked example table expanding the determinant for 3 i minus j plus 2 k crossed with i plus 2 j minus k: the i component is minus 3, the j component is 5 and the k component is 7.
visual.caption: Result $-3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$, and it is perpendicular to both.

slides.narration: Write i, j and k in the top row and the two vectors below. Expand along the top row. The i part is minus three, the j part, after its minus sign, is five, and the k part is seven. Check by dotting the answer with each vector: both give zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: a perpendicular unit vector
slides.body_md: Find a unit vector along which a camera can point at right angles to two edges.
slides.narration: Find the cross product, then divide it by its own magnitude.

slides.heading: Areas from the vector product
slides.body_md: The parallelogram on $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ has area base $\times$ height $= |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$.

visual.alt: Area by the vector product: a parallelogram O A C B on sides a and b with angle theta at O; the dashed height from B meets the base O A at H with a right angle, so the height is the magnitude of b times sine theta.
visual.caption: Area $= |\vec{a}| \cdot |\vec{b}|\sin\theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; a triangle on the same sides has half of it.

slides.narration: The area of a parallelogram is base times height. With sides a and b and angle theta between them, the height is the magnitude of b times sine theta. So the area is the magnitude of a cross b. A triangle on the same two sides has half that area.

slides.heading: Area formulas
slides.body_md: One cross product, then halve if needed.

visual.alt: Table of area formulas with the vector product: a parallelogram on adjacent sides a and b has area the magnitude of a cross b, a triangle on the same sides has half of it, a triangle A B C uses AB cross AC, and a parallelogram given by its diagonals has half the magnitude of their cross product.
visual.caption: Halve for a triangle; halve again never.

slides.narration: For a triangle with corners A, B and C, take the vectors along two sides from the same corner, find their cross product, and halve its magnitude. For a parallelogram given by its diagonals, the area is half the magnitude of the cross product of the diagonals.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: area of a triangle
slides.body_md: Find the area of the triangle with corners $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$ and $C(0, 0, 3)$.

visual.alt: Worked example table for the triangle with corners on the axes at 1, 2 and 3: the side vectors are minus i plus 2 j and minus i plus 3 k, their cross product is 6 i plus 3 j plus 2 k of magnitude 7, so the area is seven halves.
visual.caption: A triangle with one corner on each axis.

slides.narration: From corner A the sides are minus i plus two j and minus i plus three k. Their cross product is six i plus three j plus two k, whose magnitude is seven. Half of seven, seven halves, is the area of the triangle.

slides.heading: Collinearity by the vector product
slides.body_md: Non-zero $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel exactly when $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$; points $A, B, C$ are collinear when $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{0}$.

visual.alt: Table of properties of the vector product: its magnitude uses the sine of the angle, it is perpendicular to both vectors by the right-hand rule, reversing the order changes the sign, the cyclic products of the unit vectors, and the product of parallel vectors is the zero vector.
visual.caption: The answer is a vector.

slides.narration: When two vectors are parallel the angle between them is zero or a straight angle, and its sine is zero, so the cross product is the zero vector. Three points are collinear when the cross product of two side vectors from one of them is zero: the triangle they make has no area.

slides.heading: Quick check: area of a glass pane
slides.body_md: Find the area of a triangular pane from its three corners.
slides.narration: Use two side vectors from the same corner and halve the magnitude of their cross product.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is a number; $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is a vector

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the scalar product formulas, the perpendicular test, the scalar projection, the vector product perpendicular to both vectors, and areas and collinearity from the vector product.
visual.caption: Part 2 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up: the dot product is a number that gives angles, perpendicularity and projections. The cross product is a vector perpendicular to both, whose magnitude gives areas. A zero dot product means perpendicular, and a zero cross product means parallel.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write a dot product as a vector
Expand the cross product as a **determinant**; keep the minus sign for $\hat{j}$
Halve for a triangle, not for a parallelogram

rows: dot product, magnitudes, then the angle
formula, dot product, value with sign
side vectors, cross product, magnitude, halving for a triangle

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: angle questions need the dot product, magnitudes and angle; projection questions need the formula, the dot product and the value with its sign; perpendicular unit vectors need the cross product, its magnitude and both signs; area questions need side vectors, the cross product and halving for a triangle.
visual.caption: Write the determinant before expanding it.

slides.narration: Keep the two products apart: a dot product is a number, a cross product is a vector. Write the determinant before you expand it, and do not lose the minus sign in the middle term. When asked for a unit vector perpendicular to two vectors, give both signs. And halve the area only for a triangle.

notes.title: Vector Algebra — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Vectors, magnitude and direction
sections.body_md:
A **vector** has magnitude and direction and is drawn as a directed line segment $\overrightarrow{PQ}$. For $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$:

- $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$; the **unit vector** is $\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$.
- **Direction cosines** $l, m, n$ are the cosines of the angles with the axes: $l = \dfrac{a_1}{|\vec{a}|}$ and so on, with $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.
- **Direction ratios** are any three numbers proportional to $l, m, n$, for example $a_1, a_2, a_3$.
- A vector of magnitude $k$ along $\vec{a}$ is $k\hat{a}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Cosines of the angles a vector makes with the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes.

visual.alt: Table of three vectors with their magnitudes and direction cosines: 2 i minus 6 j plus 3 k has magnitude 7, 4 i plus 4 j minus 7 k has magnitude 9, and i minus 2 j plus 2 k has magnitude 3; each direction cosine is a component divided by the magnitude.
visual.caption: Direction cosine = component ÷ magnitude.

visuals.alt: Table of formulas: the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components; the direction cosines are the components divided by the magnitude and their squares add to 1; direction ratios are any numbers proportional to the components.
visuals.caption: Ratios are proportional to the cosines; cosines are fixed.

sections.heading: 2. Types of vectors
sections.body_md:
- **Zero vector** $\vec{0}$: magnitude $0$, no definite direction.
- **Unit vector:** magnitude $1$.
- **Equal vectors:** same magnitude and same direction (wherever drawn).
- **Negative of a vector:** same magnitude, opposite direction; $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$.
- **Collinear (parallel) vectors:** $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$ for a scalar $\lambda$ — like when $\lambda > 0$, opposite when $\lambda < 0$. In components, the ratios $\dfrac{b_1}{a_1} = \dfrac{b_2}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_3}{a_3}$ are equal.

key_terms.definition_md: Vectors along parallel lines; one is a scalar multiple of the other.

rows: one is a scalar multiple of the other

visual.alt: Table of types of vectors: the zero vector has magnitude 0, a unit vector has magnitude 1, equal vectors share magnitude and direction, the negative of a vector reverses its direction, and collinear vectors are scalar multiples of each other.
visual.caption: Collinear vectors may point the same way or opposite ways.

sections.heading: 3. Position vectors and operations
sections.body_md:
The **position vector** of $A(x, y, z)$ is $\vec{a} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$, and $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$ (head minus tail).

- **Triangle law:** $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$; the parallelogram law gives the same sum as a diagonal.
- In components, add, subtract and scale **one direction at a time**.
- The distance between $A$ and $B$ is $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$.

key_terms.definition_md: The vector from the origin to a point; its components are the coordinates.

visual.alt: Position vectors from the origin O: an arrow a to the point A and an arrow b to the point B; the arrow from A to B is b minus a, head minus tail.
visual.caption: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$.

visuals.alt: Table of operations on vectors in components: the sum adds components, the difference subtracts them and a scalar multiple multiplies each component, illustrated with a equals i plus 2 j minus k and b equals 2 i minus j.
visuals.caption: Work with each of $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ separately.

visuals.alt: Triangle law of addition: an arrow a from O to A, followed by an arrow b from A to B; the arrow from O straight to B closes the triangle and is the sum a plus b.
visuals.caption: Triangle law: $\overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB}$.

sections.heading: 4. The section formula
sections.body_md:
If $R$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $m : n$:

- **internally:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}$ ($R$ between $P$ and $Q$);
- **externally:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} - n\vec{p}}{m - n}$, $m \ne n$ ($R$ on $PQ$ produced).
- **Midpoint:** $\dfrac{\vec{p} + \vec{q}}{2}$. The centroid of a triangle is $\dfrac{\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}}{3}$.
- **Collinear points:** $A, B, C$ are collinear when $\overrightarrow{AC} = \lambda\,\overrightarrow{AB}$; the ratio follows from $\lambda$.

key_terms.definition_md: Division of a segment by a point on the segment produced.

visual.alt: Section formula: a segment from P to Q with the point R on it, splitting it into parts marked m and n; dashed lines from the origin O to P, R and Q show the position vectors p, r and q.
visual.caption: $R$ divides $PQ$ internally in $m : n$ (drawn for $2 : 1$).

visuals.alt: Table of the section formulae: internal division in m to n gives m q plus n p over m plus n, between P and Q; external division gives m q minus n p over m minus n, outside the segment; the midpoint is p plus q over 2.

sections.heading: 5. The scalar (dot) product and projections
sections.body_md:
- $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$, a **scalar**; $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$; $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$.
- Angle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$; non-zero vectors are **perpendicular** iff $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$.
- $|\vec{a} \pm \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 \pm 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$.
- **Scalar projection** of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$: $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$ (negative for an obtuse angle). **Vector projection:** $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\,\vec{b}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The signed length of the shadow of $\vec{a}$ on the line of $\vec{b}$.

visual.alt: Projection: vector a from O to A makes an angle theta with vector b along the base line from O to B; a dashed perpendicular from A meets the base at M with a right angle, and the length OM is the projection of a on b.
visual.caption: $OM = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

visuals.alt: Table of properties of the scalar product: its definition with the cosine of the angle, the component formula, commutativity, the dot product of a vector with itself equal to its magnitude squared, the products of unit vectors, and the test for perpendicular vectors.
visuals.caption: The answer is a number (a scalar).

visuals.alt: Table of projections with an example: the scalar projection of a on b is the dot product divided by the magnitude of b, here minus 2; the vector projection is the dot product over the square of the magnitude times b, here minus two thirds of b.
visuals.caption: A negative projection means an obtuse angle.

sections.heading: 6. The vector (cross) product, areas and collinearity
sections.body_md:
- $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, perpendicular to both (right-hand rule); $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$.
- $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$; $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \vec{0}$.
- In components, expand $\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$.
- Unit vectors perpendicular to both: $\pm\dfrac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$.
- **Areas:** parallelogram $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; triangle $\tfrac12|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; with diagonals $\tfrac12|\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}|$.
- **Parallel / collinear:** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$. Also $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$.

key_terms.definition_md: Curl the fingers from $\vec{a}$ towards $\vec{b}$; the thumb points along $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

visual.alt: Area by the vector product: a parallelogram O A C B on sides a and b with angle theta at O; the dashed height from B meets the base O A at H with a right angle, so the height is the magnitude of b times sine theta.
visual.caption: Area $= |\vec{a}| \cdot |\vec{b}|\sin\theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; a triangle on the same sides has half of it.

visuals.alt: Table of properties of the vector product: its magnitude uses the sine of the angle, it is perpendicular to both vectors by the right-hand rule, reversing the order changes the sign, the cyclic products of the unit vectors, and the product of parallel vectors is the zero vector.
visuals.caption: The answer is a vector.

visuals.alt: Table of area formulas with the vector product: a parallelogram on adjacent sides a and b has area the magnitude of a cross b, a triangle on the same sides has half of it, a triangle A B C uses AB cross AC, and a parallelogram given by its diagonals has half the magnitude of their cross product.
visuals.caption: Halve for a triangle; halve again never.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Unit vector, direction cosines (1–2 marks):* the magnitude, then the division.
- *Section formula (2–3 marks):* the formula with the correct weights and sign, then the point.
- *Angle and projection (2–3 marks):* the dot product, the magnitudes, the value (keep its sign).
- *Perpendicular unit vector, area (3 marks):* the determinant, the cross product, its magnitude, then the unit vector (both signs) or the area (halved for a triangle).
- *Section D (5 marks):* set in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$ (it is head minus tail).
- Forgetting $m - n$ in the external section formula.
- Losing the minus sign of the $\hat{j}$ term in a cross product.
- Treating $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ as a vector, or $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{b} \times \vec{a}$.
- Dividing by $|\vec{b}|^2$ for the scalar projection (that is for the vector projection).

questions.stem_md: The taut string of a kite runs from Aarav's hand to the kite along $2\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ (in metres). How long is the string?
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-6)^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{4 + 36 + 9} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. The value $49$ forgets the square root and $11$ adds the components without squaring.

questions.stem_md: A survey drone climbs along $6\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. The direction cosines of its path are
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = 7$, so $l, m, n = \tfrac67, -\tfrac27, \tfrac37$. The numbers $6, -2, 3$ are only direction ratios, and the last option points the opposite way.

questions.stem_md: A guide rope on a tent in Ladakh points along $4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$. The unit vector along the rope is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 49} = \sqrt{81} = 9$, so $\hat{v} = \dfrac{\vec{v}}{9}$. Dividing by $81$ uses the square of the magnitude instead of the magnitude.

questions.stem_md: Two ropes pull a crate across a godown floor with forces $3\hat{i} - \hat{j}$ and $-6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$. These two vectors are
questions.solution_md: $-6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} = -2(3\hat{i} - \hat{j})$: a negative multiple, so the forces act along the same line in opposite directions. They are not equal (different magnitudes and directions), and their dot product $-18 - 2 = -20 \ne 0$.

questions.stem_md: A support beam in a planetarium dome makes equal acute angles with the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes. Each of its direction cosines equals
questions.solution_md: With $l = m = n$ and $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$, we get $3l^2 = 1$, so $l = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ (positive, since the angles are acute).

questions.stem_md: The pointer of a sundial model leans along $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \sqrt{2}\,\hat{k}$. The angle it makes with the $x$-axis is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 2} = 2$, so $l = \cos\alpha = \tfrac12$ and $\alpha = 60^\circ$. The angle with the $z$-axis, where $\cos\gamma = \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, is the $45^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A drone flies straight from the point $P(2, -1, 4)$ to the point $Q(5, 3, -2)$. The vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ = position vector of $Q$ minus that of $P$ ("head minus tail") $= (5 - 2)\hat{i} + (3 + 1)\hat{j} + (-2 - 4)\hat{k}$. The second option is $\overrightarrow{QP}$ and the third adds the position vectors.

questions.stem_md: In a game engine, $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j}$. The vector $2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}$ is
questions.solution_md: $2\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $3\vec{b} = 6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$, so $2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b} = -4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

questions.stem_md: Two successive gusts move a balloon through $2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and then $\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$ (in km). Its total displacement has magnitude
questions.solution_md: The resultant is $3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{9 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{22}$. Adding the two magnitudes $3 + \sqrt{35}$ ignores the directions.

questions.stem_md: For which value of $\lambda$ is the cable direction $\lambda\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ parallel to the pole direction $2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$?
questions.solution_md: Parallel vectors have proportional components: $\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{-3}{-2} = \dfrac32$, so $\lambda = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A footbridge in Shillong runs between pillars at $A(3, -2, 5)$ and $B(-1, 4, 1)$. A lamp is fixed at its midpoint. The position vector of the lamp is
questions.solution_md: Midpoint: $\dfrac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{2} = \dfrac{2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}}{2} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. The second option forgets to halve; the third is half of $\vec{b} - \vec{a}$.

questions.stem_md: On a straight pipeline from $P(1, -2, 3)$ to $Q(6, 8, -2)$, a valve divides $PQ$ internally in the ratio $2 : 3$. The valve is at
questions.solution_md: $\vec{r} = \dfrac{2\vec{q} + 3\vec{p}}{5} = \dfrac{(12 + 3,\ 16 - 6,\ -4 + 9)}{5} = (3, 2, 1)$. Swapping the weights gives $(4, 6, 0)$, which divides $PQ$ in $3 : 2$.

questions.stem_md: A survey peg is placed on line $PQ$ produced beyond $Q$, dividing $PQ$ externally in the ratio $3 : 1$, where $P = (2, 1, 0)$ and $Q = (4, 5, 2)$. The peg is at
questions.solution_md: External division: $\vec{r} = \dfrac{3\vec{q} - \vec{p}}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{(12 - 2,\ 15 - 1,\ 6 - 0)}{2} = (5, 7, 3)$. The point $(3.5, 4, 1.5)$ divides $PQ$ internally in $3 : 1$; forgetting to divide by $2$ gives $(10, 14, 6)$.

questions.stem_md: A climbing wall has holds at $P(2, 1, -1)$, $R(6, 5, 3)$ and $Q(8, 7, 5)$, all on one straight line. In what ratio does $R$ divide $PQ$?
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{PR} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{RQ} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, so $\overrightarrow{PR} = 2\,\overrightarrow{RQ}$: $R$ lies between $P$ and $Q$ with $PR : RQ = 2 : 1$.

questions.stem_md: A fitness app stores the vectors $3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Their scalar product is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3(1) + (-2)(5) + 4(2) = 3 - 10 + 8 = 1$. A scalar product is a number, not a vector.

questions.stem_md: Two struts of a roof truss point along $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. The cosine of the angle between them is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4$ and $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 3$, so $\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{3 \times 3} = \dfrac49$.

questions.stem_md: A laser beam along $2\hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ must hit a mirror normal $3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ at right angles. Then $\lambda =$
questions.solution_md: Perpendicular means the dot product is $0$: $6 - 2\lambda + 4 = 0$, so $\lambda = 5$.

questions.stem_md: In a physics simulation, the scalar projection of $\vec{a} = 4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 8\hat{k}$ on $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 8 - 1 - 16 = -9$ and $|\vec{b}| = 3$, so the projection is $\dfrac{-9}{3} = -3$. The negative sign shows the angle between them is obtuse.

questions.stem_md: Two forces have magnitudes $|\vec{a}| = 4$ and $|\vec{b}| = 3$ newtons, and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -2$. The magnitude of their resultant $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 16 + 9 - 4 = 21$, so the resultant is $\sqrt{21}$ N. Ignoring the dot-product term gives $5$.

questions.stem_md: A robot's step $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ is split along the corridor direction $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. The vector projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3 + 2 - 2 = 3$ and $|\vec{b}|^2 = 9$, so the vector projection is $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\,\vec{b} = \dfrac39\,\vec{b} = \tfrac13(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$.

questions.stem_md: For two non-zero vectors drawn from one corner of a plot of land, $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|$. What does this tell you?
questions.solution_md: Squaring: $|\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 - 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$, so $4\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$: the vectors are perpendicular (the parallelogram on them is a rectangle with equal diagonals).

questions.stem_md: A torque calculation in a workshop needs $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ for $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. It equals
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = (6 - 0)\hat{i} - (3 - 0)\hat{j} + (1 - 0)\hat{k}$. The second option is $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$.

questions.stem_md: A solar panel is a parallelogram with adjacent edges $2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} - \hat{k}$ (in metres). Its area is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{1 + 16 + 1} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$. Halving gives the area of the triangle, not the parallelogram.

questions.stem_md: A triangular sail is tied at $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$ and $C(0, 0, 3)$. Its area in square units is
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times (-\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}) = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 4} = 7$; the area is half of this, $\dfrac72$.

questions.stem_md: A spanner applies forces where $|\vec{a}| = 6$, $|\vec{b}| = 5$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 18$. Then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| =$
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{18}{30} = \dfrac35$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac45$ and $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = 6 \times 5 \times \dfrac45 = 24$. (Check: $24^2 + 18^2 = 900 = (6 \times 5)^2$.)

questions.stem_md: A drone camera must point at right angles to both edges $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ of a rooftop. A unit vector it could point along is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, perpendicular to both; dividing by its magnitude $\sqrt{3}$ makes it a unit vector. The second option is perpendicular but not a unit vector.

questions.stem_md: Three marker buoys at $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(3, 5, 4)$ and $C(7, 11, k)$ must lie on one straight line. Then $k =$
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = 6\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + (k - 3)\hat{k}$. Collinear means $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{0}$, i.e. $\overrightarrow{AC} = 3\,\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $k - 3 = 3$ and $k = 6$.

questions.stem_md: Using the cyclic order of the unit vectors along the axes, the cross product $\hat{j} \times \hat{i}$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and swapping the order changes the sign: $\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}$. The answer is a vector, so $1$ is impossible.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The numbers $\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac12$ can be the direction cosines of a line.

**Reason (R):** The direction cosines $l, m, n$ of any line satisfy $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: R is true. Here $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac34 \ne 1$, so A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $\hat{a}$ and $\hat{b}$ are unit vectors with $\hat{a} \cdot \hat{b} = 0$, then $|\hat{a} + \hat{b}| = \sqrt{2}$.

**Reason (R):** $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ for any vectors.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: By R, $|\hat{a} + \hat{b}|^2 = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2$, which gives A. Both are true and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $(2\hat{i} + \hat{j}) \times (4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) = \vec{0}$.

**Reason (R):** The vector product of two collinear vectors is the zero vector.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} = 2(2\hat{i} + \hat{j})$, so the vectors are collinear and, by R, their cross product is $\vec{0}$ (the angle between them is $0$, and $\sin 0 = 0$). Both are true and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ for all vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

**Reason (R):** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ for all vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: The scalar product is commutative, so A is true. R is false: $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** No point divides a segment $AB$ externally in the ratio $1 : 1$.

**Reason (R):** The external section formula $\dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$ has $m - n$ in its denominator.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: With $m = n$ the denominator is $0$, so the formula breaks down: geometrically, a point outside $AB$ cannot be equally far from $A$ and $B$ while lying on the line. Both are true and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The position vector of the point $P(3, -4, 0)$ has magnitude $5$.

**Reason (R):** The magnitude of $x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ is $x + y + z$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $|3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so A is true. R is false: the magnitude is $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$ (here $x + y + z = -1$).

questions.stem_md: A diver descends straight down through $-3\hat{k}$ metres. The unit vector giving the diver's direction of motion is $-\hat{k}$.
questions.solution_md: $|-3\hat{k}| = 3$, and $\dfrac{-3\hat{k}}{3} = -\hat{k}$. True.

questions.stem_md: If $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$, then $\vec{a}$ or $\vec{b}$ must be the zero vector.
questions.solution_md: False. Non-zero perpendicular vectors also have zero dot product, for example $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\hat{i} - \hat{j}$.

questions.stem_md: The vector $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
questions.solution_md: True: by definition $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is along the normal to the plane of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, so its dot product with each of them is $0$.

questions.stem_md: The point that divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $2 : 1$ lies between $A$ and $B$.
questions.solution_md: False. External division puts the point on $AB$ produced: in $2 : 1$ it lies beyond $B$, with $B$ the midpoint of $A$ and the new point.

questions.stem_md: A robot arm reaches from its base to its tip along $3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. The arm is ____ units long.
If a velocity vector $\vec{v}$ has magnitude $7$, then $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{v} =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{v} = |\vec{v}|^2 = 49$.

questions.stem_md: Completing the cyclic rule for the axis unit vectors: $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = $ ____ (write the unit vector).
questions.solution_md: In the cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k}$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$ (written k).

questions.stem_md: A wind-sock points along $\vec{a} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. For which positive number $k$ does $k\vec{a}$ have magnitude $12$?
Two mobile towers stand at $P(1, 2, -1)$ and $Q(3, -4, 2)$ (in km). Find the straight-line distance between them in km.
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = 2\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, so $PQ = \sqrt{4 + 36 + 9} = 7$ km.

questions.stem_md: A triangular park has corners $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(4, -1, 0)$ and $C(-2, 5, 6)$. A fountain is at the centroid $G$, whose position vector is $\tfrac13(\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c})$. Find the sum of the coordinates of $G$.
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = 3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$, so $G = (1, 2, 3)$ and the sum is $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$.

questions.stem_md: Two roof rafters point along $3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}$. Find the angle between them in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 9$ and $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 3\sqrt{2}$, so $\cos\theta = \dfrac{9}{18} = \dfrac12$ and $\theta = 60^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A constant force $\vec{F} = 4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ newtons pushes a trolley from the point $(1, 2, 0)$ to the point $(3, 5, 4)$ (in metres). The work done is $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$, where $\vec{d}$ is the displacement. Find the work in joules.
A triangular glass pane has corners $A(1, 1, 1)$, $B(2, 3, 1)$ and $C(3, 1, 3)$ (in feet). Find its area in square feet.
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) \times (2\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}) = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$, of magnitude $6$; the area is $\tfrac12 \times 6 = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A zip-line cable runs along $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. Find the unit vector along the cable and its direction cosines.

answer.model_answer_md:
$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$, so $\hat{a} = \tfrac17(2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k})$.

The direction cosines are $\tfrac27, -\tfrac37, \tfrac67$.

questions.solution_md: Divide by the magnitude; the components of the unit vector are the direction cosines.

questions.stem_md: A delivery drone hops from the depot $P(-1, 3, 2)$ to a rooftop $Q(4, 0, -2)$. Write $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ in component form and find the length of the hop.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\overrightarrow{PQ} = (4 + 1)\hat{i} + (0 - 3)\hat{j} + (-2 - 2)\hat{k} = 5\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$.

$|\overrightarrow{PQ}| = \sqrt{25 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Head minus tail, then the magnitude.

questions.stem_md: A ship must sail $9$ nautical miles in the direction of $2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$. Write its displacement vector.

answer.model_answer_md:
$|2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$, so the unit vector is $\tfrac13(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k})$.

Displacement $= 9 \times \tfrac13(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$.

questions.solution_md: Magnitude times the unit vector.

questions.stem_md: A tunnel is dug from $A(4, 1, -2)$ to $B(-2, 7, 4)$. A ventilation shaft is placed at the point dividing $AB$ internally in the ratio $1 : 2$. Find its position vector.

answer.model_answer_md: $\vec{r} = \dfrac{1 \cdot \vec{b} + 2 \cdot \vec{a}}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{(-2 + 8)\hat{i} + (7 + 2)\hat{j} + (4 - 4)\hat{k}}{3} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$.

questions.solution_md: r = (m b + n a)/(m + n) with m : n = 1 : 2.

questions.stem_md: A boundary wall from $A(1, 2, -1)$ to $B(3, 0, 1)$ is extended beyond $B$ to a gate $C$ that divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $3 : 2$. Find the position vector of the gate.
questions.solution_md: External division: subtract the weighted vectors and divide by m − n.

questions.stem_md: Two brackets on a frame point along $\lambda\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$. Find $\lambda$ if the brackets are at right angles.

answer.model_answer_md:
Perpendicular, so the dot product is zero: $3\lambda + 2\lambda - 4 = 0$.

$5\lambda = 4$, so $\lambda = \dfrac45$.

questions.solution_md: Set the scalar product to zero.

questions.stem_md: A slope-stability sensor resolves $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ along the hillside direction $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Find the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ and say what its sign means.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 2 - 6 - 2 = -6$ and $|\vec{b}| = 3$, so the projection is $\dfrac{-6}{3} = -2$.

The negative sign means the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is obtuse: $\vec{a}$ has a component of length $2$ opposite to $\vec{b}$.

questions.solution_md: a · b divided by |b|.

questions.stem_md: For a lever on a bicycle crank, $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$. Find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and its magnitude.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = (1 - 4)\hat{i} - (-3 - 2)\hat{j} + (6 + 1)\hat{k} = -3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$.

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \sqrt{9 + 25 + 49} = \sqrt{83}$.

questions.solution_md: Expand the determinant along the first row.

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram-shaped flower bed are $3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ (in metres). Find the area of the bed.

answer.model_answer_md:
Area $= \tfrac12 |\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}|$.

$\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2} = (4 - 6)\hat{i} - (12 + 2)\hat{j} + (-9 - 1)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 10\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{4 + 196 + 100} = \sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}$.

Area $= 5\sqrt{3}$ m².

questions.solution_md: With diagonals, the area is half the magnitude of their cross product.

questions.stem_md: Three survey stakes are at $A(1, 0, 2)$, $B(3, 1, 0)$ and $C(4, 1, 1)$. Using vectors, show that they form a right-angled triangle, and name the right angle.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{BC} = \hat{i} + \hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$.

$\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{BC} = 2 + 0 - 2 = 0$, so $AB \perp BC$.

The points are not collinear ($\overrightarrow{AC}$ is not a multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$), so $ABC$ is a triangle with the right angle at $B$. Check: $|AB|^2 + |BC|^2 = 9 + 2 = 11 = |AC|^2$.

questions.solution_md: Find the side vectors and look for a zero dot product.

marking_scheme.step: Right angle at B (with a check)

questions.stem_md: A rope of length $14$ m is stretched along a direction whose direction ratios are $2, 3, -6$. Find the vector(s) representing the rope and its direction cosines.

answer.model_answer_md:
A vector along the direction is $2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$.

Direction cosines: $\pm\left(\tfrac27, \tfrac37, -\tfrac67\right)$.

The rope vector is $14 \times \tfrac17(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}) = 4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 12\hat{k}$, or its negative $-4\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$ for the opposite sense.

questions.solution_md: Normalise the direction ratios, then scale to length 14.

questions.stem_md: Find $x$ and $y$ if the vectors $(x + y)\hat{i} + (2x - y)\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ record the same displacement of a parcel, and then find the magnitude of that displacement.

answer.model_answer_md:
Equal vectors have equal components: $x + y = 5$ and $2x - y = 4$.

Adding, $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$ and $y = 2$.

The displacement is $5\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{25 + 16 + 9} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$.

questions.solution_md: Equate components, solve, then find the magnitude.

questions.stem_md: A highway runs straight through towns $A(1, 2, -3)$ and $B(4, -1, 3)$. A fuel station $R$ divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $2 : 1$, and a toll plaza $S$ divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $2 : 1$. Find the position vectors of $R$ and $S$, and the ratio in which $B$ divides $RS$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{r} = \dfrac{2\vec{b} + \vec{a}}{3} = \dfrac{(8 + 1)\hat{i} + (-2 + 2)\hat{j} + (6 - 3)\hat{k}}{3} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{k}$.

$\vec{s} = \dfrac{2\vec{b} - \vec{a}}{2 - 1} = 7\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$.

$\overrightarrow{RB} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{BS} = 3\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k} = 3\,\overrightarrow{RB}$, so $B$ divides $RS$ internally in the ratio $1 : 3$.

questions.solution_md: Use both section formulae, then compare RB and BS.

questions.stem_md: Three lamp posts on a straight promenade are planned at $A(2, 3, -4)$, $B(1, -2, 3)$ and $C(4, 13, -18)$. Show that they are collinear and find the ratio in which $A$ divides $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\overrightarrow{BA} = \hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = 2\hat{i} + 10\hat{j} - 14\hat{k} = 2\,\overrightarrow{BA}$.

So $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ are parallel and share the point $A$: $B$, $A$, $C$ are collinear.

Since $\overrightarrow{AC} = 2\,\overrightarrow{BA}$ in the same direction, $A$ lies between $B$ and $C$ with $BA : AC = 1 : 2$.

questions.solution_md: Show one segment vector is a multiple of the other and read the ratio.

marking_scheme.step: Parallel with a common point, so collinear

questions.stem_md: Three forces in a tug-of-war knot balance, so $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0}$, with magnitudes $|\vec{a}| = 5$, $|\vec{b}| = 8$ and $|\vec{c}| = 7$. Find the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{c} = -(\vec{a} + \vec{b})$, so $|\vec{c}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$.

$49 = 25 + 64 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$, so $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -20$.

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{-20}{5 \times 8} = -\dfrac12$, so $\theta = 120^\circ$ $\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$.

questions.solution_md: Square c = −(a + b) to find a · b.

questions.stem_md: A crane's load moves along $\vec{a} = 4\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ while the jib points along $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$. Find the scalar and vector projections of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 8 - 2 - 3 = 3$ and $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$.

Scalar projection $= \dfrac{3}{3} = 1$.

Vector projection $= \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\,\vec{b} = \dfrac39\,\vec{b} = \tfrac13(2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

questions.solution_md: Scalar: a · b / |b|; vector: (a · b / |b|²) b.

questions.stem_md: A satellite dish must face at right angles to two support rods along $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Find a unit vector perpendicular to both rods.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = (2 - 1)\hat{i} - (4 + 1)\hat{j} + (-2 - 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \sqrt{1 + 25 + 9} = \sqrt{35}$.

Unit vectors: $\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{35}}(\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 3\hat{k})$.

questions.solution_md: Cross product, then divide by its magnitude; both signs work.

questions.stem_md: A gardener ropes off a triangular herb patch with corners $A(2, 1, 1)$, $B(3, -1, 4)$ and $C(1, 2, 0)$. Find the area of the patch.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$.

$\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (2 - 3)\hat{i} - (-1 + 3)\hat{j} + (1 - 2)\hat{k} = -\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{6}$.

Area $= \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2}$ square units.

questions.solution_md: Half the magnitude of the cross product of two side vectors.

questions.stem_md: For the vectors $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}$ used in a navigation exercise, verify that $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3 + 0 - 8 = -5$.

$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (8 - 0)\hat{i} - (4 + 6)\hat{j} + (0 - 6)\hat{k} = 8\hat{i} - 10\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, so $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 = 64 + 100 + 36 = 200$.

Left side $= 200 + 25 = 225$; right side $= |\vec{a}|^2 |\vec{b}|^2 = 9 \times 25 = 225$. Verified.

questions.solution_md: Compute both products and both magnitudes, then compare.

questions.stem_md:
A drone takes off from the origin $O$ to a hover point $A(2, -1, 2)$ and then flies the leg $\overrightarrow{AB} = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ (in hundreds of metres).

(a) Find the position vector of $B$, the distance $OB$, and the direction cosines of $\overrightarrow{OB}$. [3]

(b) Find the unit vector along $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and the vector of magnitude $10$ along $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{b} = \vec{a} + \overrightarrow{AB} = (2 + 4)\hat{i} + (-1 + 4)\hat{j} + (2 - 2)\hat{k} = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$.

$OB = \sqrt{36 + 9} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$ (hundred metres).

Direction cosines of $\overrightarrow{OB}$: $\dfrac{6}{3\sqrt{5}}, \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{5}}, 0 = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, 0$.

**(b)** $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 4} = 6$, so the unit vector is $\tfrac16(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = \tfrac13(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})$.

The vector of magnitude $10$ is $\tfrac{10}{3}(2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k})$.

questions.solution_md: Add the vectors for B, then normalise each direction.

questions.stem_md:
A metro line is planned straight through stations $A(2, -3, 4)$ and $B(8, 0, -2)$.

(a) Find the station $P$ that divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $1 : 2$ and the depot $Q$ that divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $1 : 2$. [3]

(b) Show that $Q$, $A$ and $P$ are collinear and find the ratio in which $A$ divides $QP$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{p} = \dfrac{1 \cdot \vec{b} + 2\vec{a}}{3} = \dfrac{(8 + 4)\hat{i} + (0 - 6)\hat{j} + (-2 + 8)\hat{k}}{3} = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, so $P = (4, -2, 2)$.

$\vec{q} = \dfrac{1 \cdot \vec{b} - 2\vec{a}}{1 - 2} = 2\vec{a} - \vec{b} = -4\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 10\hat{k}$, so $Q = (-4, -6, 10)$.

**(b)** $\overrightarrow{QA} = 6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, so $\overrightarrow{QA} = 3\,\overrightarrow{AP}$.

The vectors are parallel with the common point $A$, so $Q$, $A$, $P$ are collinear, and $A$ divides $QP$ internally in the ratio $3 : 1$.

questions.solution_md: Internal and external section formulae, then compare QA with AP.

marking_scheme.step: Correct use of m − n for external division

questions.stem_md:
In a robotics lab, a gripper moves along $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and a conveyor belt runs along $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

(a) Find the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, leaving your answer as an inverse cosine. [2]

(b) Find the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$, and the value of $\lambda$ for which $\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b}$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 6 - 6 - 4 = -4$, $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} = 7$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$.

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{-4}{21}$, so $\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{4}{21}\right)$, an obtuse angle.

**(b)** Scalar projection $= \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = -\dfrac43$.

$(\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}) \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \lambda|\vec{b}|^2 = -4 + 9\lambda = 0$, so $\lambda = \dfrac49$.

questions.solution_md: Dot product and magnitudes; then set (a + λb) · b = 0.

questions.stem_md:
A triangular roof panel has corners $A(1, 1, 2)$, $B(2, 3, 5)$ and $C(1, 5, 5)$ (in metres).

(a) Find the area of the panel. [3]

(b) Find a unit vector perpendicular to the panel, and the length of the perpendicular from $A$ to the edge $BC$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

$\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (6 - 12)\hat{i} - (3 - 0)\hat{j} + (4 - 0)\hat{k} = -6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{61}$.

Area $= \dfrac{\sqrt{61}}{2}$ m².

**(b)** Unit normal: $\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{61}}(-6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$.

$|\overrightarrow{BC}| = |-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}| = \sqrt{5}$. Area $= \tfrac12 \times BC \times h$, so $h = \dfrac{2 \times \tfrac{\sqrt{61}}{2}}{\sqrt{5}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{61}{5}}$ m.

questions.solution_md: Cross product of two edges for the area and the normal; then area = ½ × base × height.

questions.stem_md:
Three beacons on a hill are at $A(1, 0, 1)$, $B(3, 2, 1)$ and $C(2, 1, 4)$.

(a) Find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}|$ and the cosine of the angle $BAC$. [3]

(b) Find the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ on $\overrightarrow{AB}$, and the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $AB$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\overrightarrow{AB} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$; $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = 2\sqrt{2}$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}| = \sqrt{11}$.

$\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 2 + 2 + 0 = 4$, so $\cos A = \dfrac{4}{2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{11}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{22}}$.

**(b)** Projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ on $\overrightarrow{AB}$ $= \dfrac{4}{2\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$.

$\overrightarrow{AF} = \dfrac{4}{8}\,\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$, so $F = (2, 1, 1)$. Check: $\overrightarrow{FC} = 3\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{FC} \cdot \overrightarrow{AB} = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Dot product for the angle; vector projection for the foot of the perpendicular.

questions.stem_md:
In a 3-D modelling app, $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = -4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = \hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

(a) Show that $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are collinear and that $\vec{c}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$. [2]

(b) Find the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$, and check it using $|\vec{a}||\vec{c}|$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{b} = -2\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are collinear (opposite in direction). $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = 2 - 5 + 3 = 0$, so $\vec{c} \perp \vec{a}$.

**(b)** $\vec{a} \times \vec{c} = (-1 - 15)\hat{i} - (2 - 3)\hat{j} + (10 + 1)\hat{k} = -16\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 11\hat{k}$.

Area $= \sqrt{256 + 1 + 121} = \sqrt{378} = 3\sqrt{42}$ square units.

Check: since $\vec{a} \perp \vec{c}$, $\sin\theta = 1$ and the area is $|\vec{a}||\vec{c}| = \sqrt{14}\sqrt{27} = \sqrt{378}$.

questions.solution_md: A multiple shows collinearity; a zero dot product shows perpendicularity; the cross product gives the area.
